meta.blurb: In the desert city of Oshenar every drop of water is counted. When the Deep Well starts to fall and her father vanishes, young Ysra Vell crosses the Glass Desert with a wind-reader to find out who is stealing the city's river.
meta.bible: Ysra Vell: sixteen, daughter of a water merchant in Oshenar, sharp with numbers, honest, stubborn, learns to read the desert. Dorin Vell: her father, a kind water merchant who believes that water is a promise. Rhodric Stane: the Guildmaster of the Well-Guild, polished and greedy, who steals the river. Teyo: nineteen, a Sandwright wind-reader and guide, funny, calm, never in a hurry. Granny Orla: an old water-seller who gives Ysra a map. Pebble: Ysra's patient strider, a long-legged desert riding beast. Oshenar: the city built around the Deep Well. Deep Well: the city's only well, with a rope marked in hands. Silver Vein: the ancient underground river that feeds the well. Glass Desert: the wide desert north of the city, where storms fuse sand into glass. Dry Sea: the old name for the sand plain. Stone Gate: an old gate in a cliff, where the Silver Vein is held back by a sluice. Channelwrights: the old engineers who built the channels and painted murals. Sandwrights: the desert travellers who read wind and share water by law. Well-Guild: the guild that runs the city's water. Open Well Law: the new law of fair, shared water. Brass Cup: the Vell family's measuring cup, which becomes the city's measure. Dew-sail: a cloth that gathers dew. Glass storm: a hot storm that throws glassy sand. Sunrise Gate: the city's east gate. Cold Springs: the northern springs Dorin goes to check. Voice and tone: clear, warm and tense; desert survival told with true, simple science (dew, shade, aquifers, evaporation); the villain is greed, nobody dies, and the ending is hopeful.

beats.scene: A girl fills clay jars on a rooftop as dawn lights a shining city
beats.summary: At dawn in Oshenar, Ysra Vell fills water jars on her rooftop above a city built round one well.

beats.scene: Dorin Vell measures water into a small brass cup for a customer
beats.summary: Her father Dorin, a water merchant, measures every sale with the family's brass cup and says water is a promise.

beats.scene: Ysra and her father lean over the well and look at a marked rope
beats.summary: The rope in the Deep Well shows the water is lower than ever before.

beats.scene: A man in rich robes speaks to a restless market crowd
beats.summary: Guildmaster Rhodric Stane tells the market that the well is failing and doubles the price of water.

beats.scene: Ysra peers over a wall at a green garden full of palms and fountains
beats.summary: Ysra sees that Stane's own garden is green and his carts carry full barrels at night.

beats.scene: Dorin unrolls an old cracked map showing a thin silver line below a desert
beats.summary: Dorin tells Ysra about the Silver Vein, the ancient river that feeds the well, and says he must check the Cold Springs.

beats.scene: A caravan of tall riding beasts leaves the city gate at sunrise
beats.summary: Dorin leaves with a small caravan at dawn and gives Ysra the brass cup to keep the shop.

beats.scene: Ysra stands alone at the shop window, watching a quiet road
beats.summary: Twelve days pass and Dorin does not return; a driver comes back and says the caravan was turned away near the old road.

beats.scene: A thin man in a grey coat leans over the shop counter, smiling coldly
beats.summary: Stane's agent offers to buy the Vell shop cheaply, and Ysra refuses.

beats.scene: Ysra pours her last water into a child's cup
beats.summary: Ysra shares her last jar with hungry neighbours and decides to find her father herself.

beats.scene: An old woman presses a folded map into Ysra's hand beside a small fountain
beats.summary: Granny Orla, an old water-seller, gives Ysra a hand-drawn map of the Silver Vein and warns her about the Glass Desert.

beats.scene: Ysra bargains with a young man in a blue robe outside the wall
beats.summary: Ysra finds Teyo, a Sandwright wind-reader, who agrees to guide her for her father's best dew-sail.

beats.scene: Ysra packs water skins and a folded cloth on a patient riding beast
beats.summary: Ysra and Teyo prepare water skins, the dew-sail and her strider, Pebble.

beats.scene: Ysra hides under a cloth on a strider as guards search the gate
beats.summary: They leave at night through the Sunrise Gate, where Teyo hides Ysra from Stane's guards.

beats.scene: Two riders cross a wide pale desert under a huge star-filled sky
beats.summary: Teyo teaches Ysra to travel by night and rest in shade by day to save water.

beats.scene: Ysra tastes dew from a cloth stretched over sand at sunrise
beats.summary: At dawn Teyo shows how the dew-sail gathers water from the cold night air, and Ysra tastes her first drops.

beats.scene: Teyo points at wavy lines in the sand while Ysra crouches to look
beats.summary: Teyo teaches Ysra to read the ripples in the sand, which show the wind's direction and the way to go.

beats.scene: Deep wheel ruts and many hoofprints cross the sand toward a distant cliff
beats.summary: They find deep wheel ruts of heavy carts heading east toward the Stone Gate, with the barrels full on the way out.

beats.scene: Two figures sit by a small fire under a thousand stars
beats.summary: At night Teyo tells Ysra the Sandwright law: water belongs to whoever needs it, and is shared from the first day.

beats.scene: A copper-coloured sky looms over the desert as the riders hurry toward rocks
beats.summary: A glass storm approaches, a hot wind that throws glassy sand, and Teyo leads them to shelter in a hollow.

beats.scene: Riders and animals huddle in a rocky hollow as the storm roars
beats.summary: They shelter in the hollow while the storm roars for hours, and the striders stay calm because Ysra sings to Pebble.

beats.scene: A changed desert with new dunes where the old landmarks used to be
beats.summary: After the storm the dunes have moved and landmarks are gone, so Ysra navigates by the star and the ripples.

beats.scene: Ysra tilts a nearly empty water skin while Teyo shakes his head
beats.summary: Water runs low and Ysra wants to drink it all; Teyo teaches her to sip slowly and keep resting.

beats.scene: An old woman fills a cup from a hidden rock pool
beats.summary: At a hidden Sandwright rock pool an old keeper shares water freely and tells them Stane's carts have passed for months.

beats.scene: A tall carved stone pillar stands half buried in sand beneath the sun
beats.summary: They find an old pillar of the Channelwrights marking the line of the Silver Vein.

beats.scene: A shining blue lake appears on the horizon while Teyo grabs Ysra's arm
beats.summary: A mirage of a lake appears; Ysra runs toward it and Teyo catches her, explaining how hot air bends light.

beats.scene: A high cliff with a huge iron-barred stone gate and a few tents below
beats.summary: They reach the Stone Gate, a vast old gate in a cliff, with new iron locks and a Guild outpost beside it.

beats.scene: Ysra lies on a dune peering through a small brass spyglass
beats.summary: From a dune Ysra and Teyo watch the outpost and see barrels, a reservoir and winch-men.

beats.scene: Dorin sits tied beside a strider under a canvas awning
beats.summary: Through the spyglass Ysra sees her father's strider tied outside a hut, and then Dorin himself, alive but thin.

beats.scene: Teyo whistles on a high dune while guards run toward the sound
beats.summary: That night Teyo draws the guards away with whistles and wind tricks while Ysra creeps toward the hut.

beats.scene: Ysra kneels beside her father in a dim storeroom and he holds her face
beats.summary: Ysra finds her father, who tells her that the Guildmaster closed the Stone Gate to starve the city and store the river water for himself.

beats.scene: The Guildmaster in fine desert robes arrives on a sand skiff with guards
beats.summary: Stane arrives at the outpost and offers Ysra a share of his wealth if she stays quiet; she refuses.

beats.scene: Three figures run along a torch-lit cliff path while guards chase
beats.summary: Stane orders his guards to seize them, and Ysra, Dorin and Teyo run into the old tunnel beneath the Stone Gate.

beats.scene: A vaulted tunnel with painted walls shows a map of rivers by torchlight
beats.summary: In the tunnel Ysra finds the Channelwrights' murals, which show how the whole river system works.

beats.scene: A great iron wheel wrapped in chains stands in a dark chamber
beats.summary: They find the sluice wheel chained and locked with Stane's lock, but the mural shows a second, hidden drain wheel.

beats.scene: Ysra and Teyo heave together on a small wheel set low in the wall
beats.summary: They find the hidden second wheel behind a loose stone and turn it together, though it is stiff with age.

beats.scene: A rush of silver water pours out of a stone channel into a cavern
beats.summary: The Stone Gate opens a little, and the Silver Vein rushes through; the three climb to a high ledge as the tunnel floods.

beats.scene: A wide silver river pours through a channel in the open desert at dawn
beats.summary: The river runs free across the desert toward Oshenar, and Stane's reservoir empties into the channel.

beats.scene: Workers lower their tools as the Guildmaster shouts at them beside a river
beats.summary: Stane orders the workers to close the gate again, but they refuse, because they are thirsty too.

beats.scene: Riders follow a river with new green shoots toward a far city
beats.summary: Stane rides home to cover his tracks, and Ysra, her father and Teyo follow the river back to Oshenar.

beats.scene: A crowd gathers at a deep stone well as the rope reaches the water
beats.summary: Five days later the Deep Well begins to rise, and the crowd cheers as the rope shows more water than in months.

beats.scene: Stane stands before a hushed crowd with raised hands in the square
beats.summary: Stane claims he saved the city by opening the river; Ysra, Dorin and Teyo arrive with workers who tell the truth.

beats.scene: Elders at a long table listen to Ysra, maps spread out
beats.summary: The Well-Council hears the evidence of the tracks, the locks, the mural and Dorin's story, and strips Stane of his office.

beats.scene: Ysra speaks to the council as a chart of weights hangs behind her
beats.summary: Ysra proposes the Open Well Law: the well is measured in public, every household gets a fair share, and the Stone Gate is guarded by the city and the Sandwrights together.

beats.scene: People queue with cups beside a brass measuring cup on a pillar
beats.summary: The Vell family's Brass Cup becomes the city's official measure, used by everyone for a fair cup.

beats.scene: Ysra holds out a folded cloth to Teyo at a market stall
beats.summary: Ysra gives Teyo his payment, the dew-sail, and the council invites the Sandwrights to be keepers of the desert; Teyo accepts for his people but chooses to keep wandering.

beats.scene: Dorin sits up in bed beside a window with tea while Ysra counts coins
beats.summary: Dorin recovers his strength and offers Ysra the shop; she says she will be a merchant and also the keeper of the Stone Gate.

beats.scene: Rows of palms and gardens line a wide irrigation channel in bright sun
beats.summary: Along the channel the city plants palms and gardens, and dew-sails are hung over every roof to catch the morning dew.

beats.scene: Fields of dry cracked earth beside a green channel with people sharing water
beats.summary: A year later a drought comes, but the Open Well Law and the shared river carry the city through.

beats.scene: Ysra fills her clay jars on a rooftop above a green city
beats.summary: At dawn Ysra again fills her jars on the rooftop, with a green city below and Teyo's wind on her face.

B1B2: Ysra Vell fills her clay jars on the roof as the sun rises over Oshenar. In the middle of the city lies the Deep Well, and everyone depends on it.
Ysra's father, Dorin Vell, is a water merchant, and he measures each sale with a small brass cup. He often says that water is not just a product, because it is a promise.
Each week, Ysra and her father check the rope that hangs inside the Deep Well. It is marked in hands, and the water is now a whole hand lower than it was last month.
Guildmaster Rhodric Stane stands in the market and announces that the well is failing. From today, he says, the Well-Guild must double the price of water, and the crowd groans.
Ysra walks past the Guildmaster's grand house and sees palms, flowers and a splashing fountain. That night she also notices heavy carts of full barrels rolling quietly out of his gate.

Dorin shows Ysra an old map with a thin silver line that runs beneath the desert. It shows the Silver Vein, an underground river that feeds the well, and he decides to go north to check the Cold Springs.
Dorin leaves with three long-legged striders at sunrise, and he promises to be back in twelve days. He places the brass cup in Ysra's hands and tells her to keep the shop honest.
Twelve days pass, and then fifteen, but Dorin does not return. At last one of the caravan drivers staggers into the city, saying that the caravan was turned back near the eastern road.
A thin man from the Well-Guild visits the shop and offers to buy it for a tiny price. Ysra looks him in the eye and tells him that the Vell shop will never be for sale.
In the crowded street, a thirsty child holds out a small cup, and Ysra pours her last water into it. At that moment she decides that she must find her father herself.
Old Granny Orla, who has sold water for sixty years, gives Ysra a hand-drawn map of the Silver Vein. She warns her that the Glass Desert will kill anyone who is careless.
Outside the city wall, among the Sandwright tents, Ysra finds Teyo, a young wind-reader. He agrees to guide her across the desert in return for her father's best dew-sail.
Ysra and Teyo fill the water skins, pack dried dates and roll up the dew-sail. Her strider, Pebble, is patient and long-legged, and she snorts as if she already knows the trip will be hard.

They leave by the Sunrise Gate in the dark, but the Guildmaster's guards are searching every rider. Teyo hides Ysra beneath the dew-sail and tells the guards in a bored voice that he is carrying cloth.
Teyo explains that in the desert you should travel at night and rest in the shade by day. That way, your body wastes less water, and the sun cannot cook you.
At dawn, the dew-sail is covered in tiny drops that have gathered from the cold night air. Teyo helps Ysra tip them into a skin, and she tastes the cool, clean water.
Teyo shows Ysra how to read the ripples that the wind makes in the sand. The steep side points away from the wind, so the ripples show the steady wind's direction, even when the sun is hidden.
Across the sand, Ysra and Teyo find deep wheel ruts, as though heavy carts have passed there many times. The ruts lead toward the Stone Gate, and they are far too deep for empty barrels.
By the fire that night, Teyo tells Ysra about the law of the Sandwrights. In the desert, he says, water belongs to anyone who needs it, and you share it from the first day.
The sky turns the colour of copper, and Teyo shouts that a glass storm is coming. The wind will throw sharp grains of sand that are hot enough to melt, so they must find shelter fast.
The storm roars over them for hours, and the wind sounds like a hundred shrieking voices. Ysra holds Pebble's neck and hums an old tune until the animal stops trembling.
When the storm finally ends, the dunes have moved and every landmark has disappeared. Ysra remembers Teyo's lessons, and she finds north by the ripples and the evening star.

Their water is nearly gone, and Ysra feels so thirsty that she wants to drink everything at once. Teyo shows her how to take small sips and to breathe through her nose, so that she does not lose water.
At a hidden rock pool, an old Sandwright woman gives them water and will not take a coin. She tells them that for months Stane's heavy carts have rolled past toward the Stone Gate.
At last they find a half-buried stone pillar carved with wavy lines and fish. Teyo says that it was made by the Channelwrights, the old engineers, and that it marks the line of the Silver Vein.
A shining blue lake appears on the horizon, and Ysra begins to run toward it. Teyo catches her arm and explains that it is a mirage, which hot air makes by bending light from the sky.
At the foot of a high cliff, they reach the Stone Gate, an old doorway in the rock. New iron locks hang on it, and the Guildmaster's outpost stands close by, with armed men walking in front.
Lying on a dune, Ysra studies the outpost through a small spyglass. She sees a huge reservoir behind the wall, and men filling barrels from it.
Through the spyglass, Ysra sees her father's strider tied up outside a small hut. A moment later the door opens, and she sees Dorin himself, thin and tired but alive.
That night, Teyo whistles and flaps a cloth to make the guards think the wind-spirits are loose. While they run toward the sound, Ysra crawls toward her father's hut.
Dorin cries when he sees his daughter, and he tells her what he has discovered. The Guildmaster has closed the Stone Gate on purpose, to starve the well and to sell the river's water at a high price.
Before they can leave, the Guildmaster himself arrives at the outpost in a sand skiff. He smiles at Ysra and offers her a share of his wealth, if she will promise to stay silent.
Stane orders his men to seize them, and the three run for their lives toward the cliff. They duck into a narrow tunnel beneath the Stone Gate, which the Channelwrights built long ago.
Inside the cool, damp tunnel, Ysra holds up her torch and sees bright murals painted on the walls. They are a huge map of the whole river system, with a wheel drawn beside every gate.
In a deep chamber, they find the great wheel that controls the Stone Gate, wrapped in chains and locked. But the mural shows a second, hidden wheel that the Guild has overlooked.
Behind a loose stone at the foot of the wall, Teyo finds the second wheel. It is stiff with age, but all three of them put their weight on it, and slowly it begins to turn.
Somewhere above them, the Stone Gate shudders, and a roar fills the tunnel as the Silver Vein begins to run. The three of them scramble onto a high ledge as cold, bright water floods the floor below.
At dawn, they climb out of the tunnel and see the Silver Vein flowing free along its old channel. Stane's reservoir has opened, and its water is pouring back into the river too.
Stane orders his workers to close the Stone Gate at once, but they put down their tools. They come from Oshenar, and their own families have been thirsty too.
Stane rides off to the city to make up a story, and Ysra, Dorin and Teyo follow the river back to Oshenar. Along the way, tiny green shoots are already pushing up through the wet sand.
Five days later, the rope in the Deep Well shows a rising level, and a great cheer goes up in the square. The whole city comes to see, and some people kneel down and weep.
Stane stands in the square and claims that he alone has saved the city by opening the river. Then Ysra, her father and Teyo walk in with some of his own workers, who tell the truth.
The Well-Council listens for two days to the workers, to Dorin and to Ysra with her maps. At the end, they vote to remove Stane from the Guild and to judge him in court.
Ysra proposes an Open Well Law, in which the well is measured in public and every home gets a fair share. The Stone Gate would be guarded jointly by the city and the Sandwrights.
The old brass cup that Ysra kept for her father becomes the city's official measure. Every shop and every household now uses a copy of it, so a cup of water is the same for everyone.
Ysra offers Teyo his payment, the dew-sail, but he laughs and gives it back. The council invites the Sandwrights to keep the desert wells with the city, and Teyo says his people will gladly accept.
Dorin slowly recovers his strength, and he tells Ysra that the shop is hers now. She says that she will be a merchant and also a keeper of the Stone Gate, because both are promises.
Along the river channel, the people of Oshenar plant palms and small gardens. They also hang dew-sails over every roof, because Ysra has taught them that no drop should be wasted.
A year later a long drought dries the whole desert, and the old Oshenar would have suffered terribly. This time, the shared river, the dew-sails and the Open Well Law help every household to survive.
Ysra stands on the roof again at dawn, filling her clay jars as the sun rises. Below her the city is green and awake, and a familiar wind from the desert brings Teyo's whistle.
C1C2: At dawn, as the sun slid gold over the flat roofs of Oshenar, sixteen-year-old Ysra Vell carried clay jars up to her family's roof to catch the first cool air. Beyond the last wall the desert stretched away, pale and empty to the edge of the sky, and in the centre of the city the Deep Well sat like a stone heart that every home depended on. Nobody in Oshenar ever forgot that fact, because in that dry country every single drop was counted and weighed.

Her father, Dorin Vell, sold water in a small shop beside the market, and he measured every sale with the same old brass cup that his own grandmother had used. Water is not a product, he liked to tell his customers, but a promise, and a promise sold unfairly is only a lie that has been poured into a jar. Ysra, who was good with numbers, loved her father's cup almost as much as she loved the man himself.

Each week Ysra and her father lowered a knotted rope into the Deep Well, where every knot marked the depth of one hand, and every week they wrote down the number in a small book. This month the water stood a whole hand lower than at the start of spring, and then, a week later, half a hand lower again. Ysra did the sums three times, hoping that she had made a mistake, but the numbers stayed the same.

In the crowded market Guildmaster Rhodric Stane climbed upon a platform and announced, in the soft, regretful voice of a man who hated to give bad news, that the Deep Well was failing. For the good of the city, he said, the Well-Guild must now double the price of every cup of water, and he begged the people to be patient. A long, low groan rolled through the crowd like wind through dry grass, and nobody dared to argue with him.

Walking home, Ysra passed the Guildmaster's grand house and saw through the gate a garden of palms, roses and a splashing fountain, as green as a picture from a fairy tale. Later that night she woke to the creak of wheels and, looking from her window, watched heavy carts piled with full barrels roll quietly out of his courtyard toward the east. A man who believed that his well was dying, she thought, would not be wasting water on roses.

That evening Dorin unrolled an old map, cracked at the folds, on which a thin silver line wandered beneath the desert and ended at the centre of Oshenar. This was the Silver Vein, he explained, a hidden river that had filled the Deep Well since before the city was built, and if it were weakening, the cause would lie somewhere along its length. He would travel north with a small caravan to look at the Cold Springs, where the river was said to begin.

At sunrise Dorin Vell rode out of the Sunrise Gate with a small caravan of three long-legged striders, promising that he would be home in twelve days. Before leaving he pressed the brass cup into his daughter's hands and told her, with a smile that did not quite hide his worry, to keep the shop honest until he came back. Ysra watched the dust of his caravan thin to nothing on the horizon, and the day felt oddly empty.

Twelve days passed, then fifteen, and with each sunset the road beyond the gate remained stubbornly empty, until Ysra could hardly sleep for listening. At last one of the caravan drivers staggered through the Sunrise Gate on foot, sunburnt and exhausted, and told her that armed men had stopped them on the eastern road and had taken her father somewhere he could not say. He was too frightened to speak any more, and she did not press him.

A thin man in a grey coat from the Well-Guild leaned on the counter of the Vell shop and offered, with great courtesy, to take the whole business off her hands for a very small sum. Ysra was sixteen, alone and almost penniless, and the offer was, in its way, a comfortable escape. She looked him steadily in the eye, polished the brass cup with her sleeve, and told him that the shop was a promise and would never be for sale.

In the narrow street behind the shop a thin child held out a small clay cup, and Ysra, without a moment's hesitation, emptied the last of her own water into it and watched the little face brighten. Around her, grown men stood in a patient queue with empty jars, and the price had risen again since morning. She went home that night with her mind made up, for waiting quietly and hoping for the best was no longer an option.

Old Granny Orla, who had sold water in Oshenar for sixty years and knew every secret of the city, took Ysra's hands and pressed into them a hand-drawn map of the Silver Vein, copied from one far older. The river's course, she said, led to a place called the Stone Gate, and the way there crossed the Glass Desert, which punished the careless and rarely forgave a mistake. Then she kissed Ysra's forehead and told her to take twice as much water as she thought she would need.

Beyond the city wall, among the low tents of the Sandwrights who travelled the desert and read its winds, Ysra found a lanky young man called Teyo who was lazily sharpening a knife. He listened to her story with raised eyebrows and then agreed to guide her across the Glass Desert, asking in payment only for her father's finest dew-sail, which was thin as breath and strong as rope. Ysra suspected that he was laughing at her, and also that he was exactly the right person to ask.

By the light of a single lamp Ysra and Teyo filled the leather water skins, wrapped dried dates and flat bread in cloth, and rolled the gleaming dew-sail into a long, neat tube. Her strider, whom she had named Pebble, stood by with an expression of weary patience, flicking one ear at the sound of the buckles. Teyo checked every strap twice and said that a journey is decided by its preparation, and by Pebble's mood.

At the Sunrise Gate they found the Guildmaster's guards examining every traveller by lantern light, and Ysra's heart tripped like a hurried drum. Teyo calmly draped the dew-sail over her and Pebble's baggage, yawned theatrically, and told the guards that he was a poor wind-reader carrying nothing but laundry. The guards, who disliked the smell of a Sandwright's cloak, waved him through without another look.

Teyo explained that in the Dry Sea a sensible traveller walked by night and slept by day, because in the cool dark the body lost far less water to sweat and the sun could not cook the skin. By day they stretched the dew-sail between two poles to make a shelter, and lay beneath it in the blue shade, where the air was already a few degrees cooler. Ysra, a girl who had always thought of water as something to buy, began to see it as something to keep.

At first light Teyo took Ysra to the cloth they had strung low above the sand and showed her the thousand tiny drops that had gathered on its fibres overnight. The cold sail, he said, cooled the damp night air around it until the water in the air could no longer stay hidden, and it condensed into drops that ran together. She tipped them carefully into a skin and tasted the clean, cold water, and it was the best thing she had ever drunk.

Teyo knelt and drew his fingers along a line of ripples in the sand and explained that the steeper face of each ripple always pointed away from the wind that made it. Because the desert wind blew from the same direction for weeks at a time, he said, the ripples became a compass, one that kept working long after the sun had vanished. Ysra practised until she could tell north from south with her eyes shut and her hand on the sand.

On the third morning the travellers came upon a pair of deep wheel ruts, scored into the sand and still sharp from the passing of many heavy loads. Teyo studied them with a frown, because they were deep enough to have been cut by carts loaded with full barrels, and they led away from the city, directly toward the Stone Gate on Ysra's map. It did not make sense for a man with a failing well to carry water into the empty desert.

Beside their small fire, with the stars huge and close overhead, Teyo told Ysra of the oldest law of the Sandwrights, which every child learned before learning to walk. Water, it said, belongs to whoever needs it, and whoever finds it must share, because a traveller who hoards a well is only digging his own grave in company. Ysra, remembering her father's brass cup, thought that the Sandwrights and her father would have understood each other perfectly.

Late in the afternoon the horizon turned the colour of old copper, and Teyo, sniffing the wind, announced in an unusually serious voice that a glass storm was on its way. The wind in such storms, he said, carried sand so hot and so sharp that it could melt against stone and set into green glass, and a traveller caught in the open had no chance. They urged the striders into a deep hollow between two rocks, wrapped everything in the dew-sail, and waited.

For hours the storm roared over their hiding place like a great beast, and the wind carried a shriek that seemed to come from a hundred throats at once. Ysra pressed her face into Pebble's warm neck and hummed an old lullaby that her father had sung to her, and the strider slowly stopped trembling. Beside her, Teyo kept a grip on the dew-sail and never once lost his calm smile.

When the wind finally died, the whole desert had been rearranged, with new dunes where there had been old hollows and every familiar landmark buried or blown away. For a long hour Ysra stood silent in the strange, glittering landscape, until she crouched and read the fresh ripples and then waited for the first star, as Teyo had taught her. By the time it finally appeared, pale and steady above the new horizon, she knew exactly which way was north.

By the fifth day the water skins were hanging loose, and Ysra's thirst had become a living thing that clawed at her throat and whispered that she should drink everything at once. Teyo gently took the skin from her hand, taught her to wet her lips and take only tiny sips, and reminded her to breathe through her nose and keep her mouth closed. It was the hardest lesson yet, and it was also the one that saved them.

Late that day they stumbled upon a hidden rock pool, shaded by an overhang, where an old Sandwright woman sat knitting beside a trickle of clear water. She filled their skins without a single question and refused Ysra's coin with a shake of the head, for the law of her people allowed no price on a thirsty traveller. For months, she added darkly, heavy carts from Oshenar had creaked past her pool toward the Stone Gate, and not one driver had ever stopped to ask for a cup.

On the sixth morning they found a tall stone pillar half buried in sand, its sides carved with wavering lines and tiny fish that the wind had not yet erased. Teyo said that the old people called the makers of such pillars the Channelwrights, and that they had marked the course of the Silver Vein every day's walk across the desert. Ysra pressed her palm against the cool carving, and it felt like touching her father's hand.

Shortly before noon a wide blue lake appeared on the horizon, trembling and cool, and Ysra, who had not seen so much water in her life, started to run toward it with a cry. Teyo caught her arm and explained, very gently, that the lake was only a mirage, made when the hot air near the ground bent the light of the sky until it looked like water. She sat down heavily on the hot sand and laughed until she cried, and Teyo, kindly, laughed with her.

Late that day they reached a cliff of dark stone, and set into its foot was the Stone Gate, an enormous arch carved by the Channelwrights, now fastened with new iron locks and thick chains. Beside it stood a large outpost of the Well-Guild, with armed guards pacing the roofs and a great cistern gleaming behind a wall. The Silver Vein, Ysra realised, was being held back by a gate that someone had made to stay closed.

From the top of a distant dune they lay flat on the cooling sand, and Ysra studied the outpost through Teyo's battered spyglass until her eyes ached. She counted ten guards, three winches and a vast reservoir behind the wall, from which workers were filling barrels that rolled away to the carts. Somewhere between the locked gate and that reservoir, she thought, her city's water was being turned into the Guildmaster's wealth.

Then, among the animals tethered behind a hut, Ysra recognised her father's strider, with a white patch on its nose that she had known since she was a child. A moment later a guard opened the hut's door and shoved a thin, grey, wonderfully familiar figure out into the daylight, and her breath caught in her throat. Teyo laid a steady hand upon her shoulder and said quietly that now at least they knew where to go.

Once the moon had set, Teyo crept to the far side of the camp and began to whistle the odd, low notes that Sandwrights used to call the wind, shaking a cloth until it cracked like a flag. The guards, who were Oshenar men and half believed in desert ghosts, ran toward the sound with their lanterns held high. Ysra, crawling in the darkness along the wall, reached her father's hut without anyone seeing her.

Dorin wept when his daughter slipped through the door, and then he held her face in both hands and laughed with a cracked, hoarse voice. In whispers he explained that the Stone Gate had been shut and chained on purpose by the Guildmaster, who meant to starve the Deep Well and keep the river water for himself. The men who knew had imprisoned Dorin to buy his silence, and all of Oshenar, he said, was thirsty for the sake of one man's cistern.

Before they could slip away, a trumpet sounded and Rhodric Stane himself arrived at the outpost in a long sand skiff, spreading his jewelled hands in greeting as though he had expected visitors. With a smile as smooth as glass he offered Ysra a partnership in the trade, a house on the hill and a chest of gold, if only she would agree to forget what she had seen. She looked at the gold and then at her father's thin face, and she said no.

Stane lifted one hand, and his guards poured out of the outpost with shouts and drawn swords, and the three of them ran along the foot of the cliff with no plan except to keep running. Teyo spotted a narrow opening in the rock, half hidden by a fallen slab, and they threw themselves into the old tunnel that the Channelwrights had cut beneath the Stone Gate. Behind them, in the narrow dark, the boots of the guards thundered over the stones like a rolling drum.

Inside the tunnel the air was cool, damp and sweet with the smell of old water, and when Ysra raised her torch she saw that the walls were covered in murals painted in blue and ochre. They formed a vast map of the Silver Vein and all its channels, drawn with the exactness of a master craftsman, with a small wheel marked beside each of the gates. Ysra, who read maps like other people read faces, understood the whole design in a minute.

At the end of the tunnel stood a great iron wheel, thick as a man's body, wrapped in new chains and fastened with a heavy lock that gleamed with Stane's mark. Ysra's heart sank, until she looked up at the mural beside it, where a second, smaller wheel was painted beneath the first, labelled in the old script as a drain for emergencies. Nobody in the Well-Guild had read the old murals, because nobody in the Well-Guild had cared to.

Teyo pushed aside a loose stone at the foot of the wall and uncovered a small wheel of green bronze, stiff with centuries of damp but still whole. Dorin, Ysra and Teyo took hold together and leaned their whole weight against it, while the shouts of the guards grew louder in the tunnel behind them. With a groan that seemed to come from the heart of the rock, the wheel began to turn.

High above them the Stone Gate shuddered, and a distant roar swelled into thunder as the river, held back for months, came pouring down the old channel in a wall of bright, cold water. The three of them scrambled onto a high ledge just in time, and below them the guards, who had come running into the tunnel, turned and fled up the stairs with the flood at their heels. Nobody was hurt in the end, and everybody was thoroughly, gloriously soaked from head to foot.

By dawn they climbed out into the open, blinking in the light, and saw the Silver Vein sweeping across the desert along the old channel, glittering like a long silver ribbon. Stane's private reservoir, whose gate had been swept open by the surge, was emptying into the river too, and the water ran on toward the horizon where Oshenar waited. It would take days to reach the city, but nothing could stop it now.

Stane stormed among his workers, screaming that the Stone Gate must be closed again at any price, but one by one the labourers put down their tools. They were ordinary men from Oshenar who had been told that the well was dying, and they had watched the river pour out into the sand with the same dumb wonder as everyone else. Not one of them would raise a hand to shut it again, not for gold, and not for the Guildmaster's threats.

Stane, abandoning his men, galloped back toward Oshenar with the intention of telling his version of the story before anyone else could, while Ysra, her father and Teyo followed the river at a gentler pace. All along its banks the dry desert was already stirring, with tiny green shoots pushing up through the damp sand and birds appearing from nowhere. Dorin, riding slowly because of his weakness, said that he had never seen anything so beautiful.

On the fifth day the knotted rope in the Deep Well came up wetter than it had been for months, and a murmur ran through the crowd that had gathered around the stone rim. The next morning it came up wetter still, and by the third day the water was rising by a hand every hour, and people were laughing, hugging and kneeling on the paving. The city, which had learned to be silent about water, was suddenly full of noise.

Stane, who had arrived in the city before them, stood on the platform in the middle of the square and told the crowd that thanks to his courage and wisdom the river had been freed. Just then a murmur rose, and Ysra, Dorin and Teyo pushed through the crowd with a dozen of Stane's own workers behind them. One by one the workers stepped forward and told what they had seen, and the crowd's cheers turned slowly cold.

The Well-Council gathered in the great hall and listened for two days to the evidence, which included the deep wheel tracks, the chains on the Stone Gate, Ysra's map, the paintings of the Channelwrights and Dorin's plain story. When the last witness had spoken, every member voted to strip Rhodric Stane of the Guildmaster's seal and to judge him in open court. Stane, for the first time in his long and slippery life, found that he had nothing smooth left to say.

Ysra, who had been dreading this moment, stood before the council and proposed an Open Well Law, under which the depth of the Deep Well would be measured and posted every morning in the public square. Every household would receive a fair share, no one could sell water at a price that the council had not agreed, and the Stone Gate would be guarded together by the city and the Sandwrights. Granny Orla, who sat in the front row with her stick across her knees, was the first to clap.

In the great square the council set up a stone pillar and upon it placed the Vell family's old brass cup, announcing that from that day every measure of water in Oshenar would match it. Copies of the cup were cast for every shop, every household and every well-keeper, so that a cup of water meant the same thing to a rich man and to a poor child. Dorin watched with tears in his eyes and said that the cup had never looked so bright.

Ysra held out the dew-sail that she had promised Teyo as payment, but he laughed and pushed it back into her hands, saying that a friend is not paid in cloth. The Well-Council, which had been moved by his part in the story, invited the Sandwrights to help keep the desert wells alongside the city, and Teyo accepted on behalf of his people with the grace of a prince. He would continue to wander, he said, but he promised to return with each new moon.

Under Granny Orla's herbal tea and Ysra's relentless care, Dorin regained his strength within a month, and one morning he declared that the Vell shop belonged to his daughter. She replied, after a long pause, that she would run it and the Stone Gate besides, for a merchant who understood the river was the best protector of it. He laughed and said that he had no doubt that she could manage both, and probably the whole city if she wanted.

Along the new channel the people of Oshenar planted palm trees, vegetable beds and long green hedges, and the dusty city began to wear a ribbon of green around its throat. Ysra taught everyone to hang a dew-sail on their roof, to cover wells against the sun and to reuse water wisely, and no drop in the city was ever wasted again. The children of Oshenar, who had grown up thirsty, learned to play in a garden.

A year later a terrible drought settled over the whole of the Dry Sea, and the wells of three neighbouring cities sank lower with every week of cloudless sky. In Oshenar, however, the Silver Vein still ran steadily, the cup was shared fairly, the roofs gleamed with dew-sails, and everyone took only what they needed and gave what they could spare. People from the other cities came to learn how it was done, and Ysra showed them the cup.

Once again, at dawn, Ysra carried her clay jars up to the roof and set them in a row, while the city below her woke slowly in a haze of green leaves and morning smoke. At the centre of Oshenar the Deep Well shone clear and full, and its rope was marked in hands for everyone to read. From beyond the wall came a long, low whistle on the wind, and Ysra, smiling, put the brass cup in her pocket and went down to meet her friend.
